ca_menifee_area.blurb: Menifee Area is a collection of small boulder fields around the city of Menifee, in California's Inland Empire. Lion's Den is the largest zone, on hilly, sandy ground reached through chaparral and open grassland, with most problems 10 to 15 feet tall. Double Butte Mountain, Beer Me Boulders and Canyon Hills add more. Nearly all of it is bouldering, with a few top-rope lines and a scattering of trad, aid and a lone sport slab. Grades are friendly: most problems sit between VB and V4, with only a handful from V5 up. Mild winters, roughly December through March, are the best time to visit, while summer is hot enough that early or late sessions work better.

md_catoctin_mountain_park.blurb: Catoctin Mountain Park is a wooded mountain park in Maryland, with climbing spread along its trails and overlooks at around 1,900 feet. It is overwhelmingly a bouldering destination: Gateway Trail Boulders is the largest cluster, followed by Thurmont Vista Boulders and Hog Rock, and Wolf Rock is where the small number of trad and top-rope lines are found. Problems run from VB to V9, with the bulk between V0 and V3, so there is plenty for newer boulderers and a few harder lines at the top. The roped climbs stay easy to moderate. Climbing is scattered across many small boulders rather than concentrated at one cliff, so expect some walking between sectors.

nv_oak_creek_canyon.blurb: Oak Creek Canyon is one of the most scenic canyons in the Red Rock area of southern Nevada, with climbing between roughly 4,400 and 5,500 feet. The rock is sandstone, which weakens when wet and stays damp for days after a storm. Trad is the main event, much of it multi-pitch: Solar Slab is a large south-facing buttress near the canyon mouth, and Black Orpheus Amphitheater and Cactus Flower Tower lie close by, with Eagle Wall further up. Roped grades range from 5.6 to 5.13, concentrated between 5.8 and 5.11. A good number of boulder problems, V0 to V11, are scattered through the canyon. The Blood Wall on Cactus Flower Tower faces north and suits warmer weather.

oh_mrg_southeast_aka_darkside.blurb: MRG Southeast, also called Darkside, lies on the south bank of the Mad River inside Mad River Gorge, Ohio's largest climbing area. Crags line a river trail a few minutes' walk from the lot, under a thick forest canopy that keeps the walls cool, which suits warm days. Spring through fall is the main season. The climbing is a mix: about half is bouldering, with sport a little over a third and some trad. Amusement Wall is mainly boulders, Clear Creek Crag is the sport hub, and Overpass Area and Dad's Wall add more. Sport and trad run from 5.5 to 5.12, mostly 5.10 to 5.12, and boulder problems run V0 to V8, mostly V0 to V4.

wa_mclellan_rocks.blurb: McLellan Rocks sits northwest of Spokane, on the south bank of the Spokane River in Riverside State Park, among open ponderosa pine forest. The rock is granite, in small domes and corridors around 50 feet tall. Sport climbing dominates, with a healthy amount of trad and a bouldering zone. Roped grades run from 5.4 to 5.12, with the heart of the climbing at 5.10 and 5.11, and boulder problems run from V3 up to V9. The area is split into many small walls, including Crisis Wall, Toadstool Wall, Hummel's Landing and Lost Wall. April through October is the best window: April and May are nicest, summer is hot, and most walls face east or west, so you can chase sun or shade.

az_lake_mary_areas.blurb: Lake Mary Areas is a boulder-only collection south of Flagstaff, near Lower Lake Mary. The Ridge is the main zone, a half-mile line of walls linked by the Drysdale Trail, with views over the lake and Mormon Mountain. Its rock is limestone, with bulging walls and positive holds. Smaller spots such as Walnut Creek add variety. Problems run from VB to V7, and the weight of the climbing sits between V0 and V3, so moderate climbers have plenty to work on, while the harder lines gather on a few showcase walls. Several walls are friendly to pads, but the trail itself needs occasional upkeep and monsoon rains can change it.
